label: M_k-Polyhedral Complexes
notes: This chapter, printed pages 97 through 122, builds spaces by gluing convex cells cut from a single model of constant curvature. The agenda is to define the cells, fuse them along isometric faces, equip the result with an intrinsic length metric, and read off when that metric is complete and geodesic.

label: The Model Space M_k
notes: Everything is cut from one model. For positive kappa we use a rescaled sphere, for zero kappa Euclidean space, for negative kappa rescaled hyperbolic space. Fixing kappa once means all cells share a curvature, so curvature lives only in how the cells are combinatorially assembled, not inside any single cell.

label: Convex Polyhedral Cells
notes: A cell is a compact convex polytope inside the model, the intersection of finitely many half-spaces. Its faces are again convex cells of lower dimension. These cells are the rigid Lego bricks of the theory: every metric statement about the complex is ultimately reduced to geometry inside one such convex piece.

label: Gluing Along Isometric Faces
notes: We take a disjoint family of cells and a collection of isometries identifying faces in pairs. The quotient under the generated equivalence relation is the complex. The crucial discipline is that gluing maps are isometries of faces, so the inherited Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic geometry agrees across every seam.

label: Finitely Many Shapes
notes: Shapes are isometry classes of cells. The finiteness hypothesis says only finitely many isometry types appear, even if infinitely many cells are glued. This single uniformity assumption controls the geometry near every point and is exactly what later powers the completeness and geodesic conclusions of Bridson's theorem.

label: Strings and the Intrinsic Pseudometric
notes: Distance is defined by chains of points called strings that hop through a sequence of cells, summing the within-cell distances. The pseudometric is the infimum over all admissible strings joining two points. This is the taut-string idea: the metric measures the shortest path that respects how the cells are stitched together.

label: A Taut String Across Cells
notes: The figure traces a string entering several glued cells, breaking only on shared faces, and pulling taut to the shortest admissible route. Walk the audience along it: inside each cell the segment is a model geodesic, and the broken points sit exactly on the gluing edges that join consecutive cells.

label: From Pseudometric to Metric
notes: A priori the infimum could vanish between distinct points, so we only have a pseudometric. Under finitely many shapes this degeneracy cannot happen: distinct points stay a positive distance apart. The quotient is then a genuine metric space and we may ask whether the metric is realised by paths.

label: Bridson's Theorem
notes: Bridson's theorem is the chapter's engine: an M_k-polyhedral complex with only finitely many isometry types of cells is a complete geodesic metric space. Stress both payoffs. Completeness means Cauchy sequences converge, and geodesic means any two points are joined by a shortest path realising their distance.

label: The Link of a Vertex
notes: Zoom into a vertex and record the unit directions leaving it. Each incident cell contributes a spherical cell of directions, and these glue into the link, a smaller M_1 spherical complex. The link is the infinitesimal model of the complex at that vertex and packages all of its local geometry.

label: Links Control Local Geometry
notes: The link is where curvature is tested. A neighbourhood of the vertex is a metric cone over its link, so local geodesic and curvature behaviour is governed by lengths of loops in the link. The threshold to remember is that short loops must have length at least two pi for the expected local behaviour.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the pipeline: model cells, isometric gluing, string pseudometric, finitely many shapes giving a complete geodesic space, and links as the local controllers. Looking ahead, the link condition becomes the combinatorial gateway to the CAT(kappa) curvature tests developed in the chapters that follow this one.
